title: Testing & CI/CD
tagline: Unit tests, integration tests, E2E, TDD red-green-refactor, the test pyramid, and the CI/CD pipeline — the full quality and delivery system.

sections.content:
Software that is not tested is software that is broken in ways you haven't found yet. **Testing** is the discipline of verifying correctness at multiple layers — fast isolated unit tests, realistic integration tests, and slow but thorough end-to-end tests. The **test pyramid** tells you the right ratio: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few E2E tests.

**CI/CD** (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) is the infrastructure that runs those tests automatically on every commit, builds deployable artefacts, and — in full CD — deploys them to production. Together, tests + CI/CD create a safety net that lets teams ship confidently and frequently.

flowchart TD

sections.caption: CI/CD pipeline: every push triggers automated quality gates; only green builds reach production.

sections.title: Quality Control on a Factory Line
sections.content:
**Unit tests** are like inspecting each individual component on the factory floor — check that every bolt is the right size before it ever meets another part. They are cheap, fast (milliseconds each), and pinpoint failures to a single function. **Integration tests** are like assembling a sub-system — bolt, spring, and lever — and checking they move together correctly. Slower, but they catch interface mismatches that unit tests miss.

**E2E tests** are like a test-drive of the finished car — realistic, but expensive (minutes per run) and fragile (a minor UI tweak can break a selector). **TDD's red-green-refactor** is the engineer's discipline of writing the inspection checklist *before* building the part: Red = checklist fails (part doesn't exist yet), Green = part passes inspection, Refactor = clean up the part without breaking the checklist. **CI/CD** is the conveyor belt: every commit automatically runs every inspection and only ships parts that pass all checks.

**Unit tests** test a single function or class in isolation. Dependencies are replaced with fakes (mocks, stubs, spies). They should run in milliseconds, produce deterministic results, and require no external services. A codebase with high unit-test coverage finds bugs at the cheapest possible moment — during development. In JavaScript, Jest is the dominant framework: `describe` groups related tests, `it` or `test` defines a case, `expect` asserts the result.

**Integration tests** wire together two or more real components — a service + a database, a router + a handler — and verify they collaborate correctly. They are slower (real I/O) but catch contract mismatches that mocks miss. A common pattern is an in-memory database or a test container for each test run. **End-to-End (E2E) tests** drive the actual application through a real browser or HTTP client from the user's perspective. They provide the highest confidence but are the slowest and most brittle layer — use them sparingly for critical paths (login, checkout, critical workflows).

**Test-Driven Development (TDD)** reverses the usual order: write a failing test first (Red), write the minimum production code to make it pass (Green), then improve the code without breaking tests (Refactor). This rhythm forces small, testable units and produces a test suite as a by-product of development — not an afterthought. **Code coverage** (statements, branches, functions, lines) measures what percentage of production code is exercised by tests. 80% branch coverage is a common target; 100% is rarely worth the cost.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["RED: write a failing test"]
    A --> B["RUN: test fails as expected"]
    B --> C["GREEN: write minimum code to pass"]
    C --> D["RUN: test passes"]
    D --> E["REFACTOR: clean up code"]
    E --> F["RUN: test still passes"]
    F --> A
sections.caption: TDD red-green-refactor cycle: tests drive design, and refactoring is always safe because tests guard correctness.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Each `it` block tests exactly one behaviour — happy path, edge case, or error path. The mock `httpClient` prevents real network calls in unit tests while still verifying that `fetchOrder` uses the response correctly. Note: `toBeCloseTo` is preferred over `toBe` for floating-point assertions. The TDD flow here would be: write the `it` blocks first (Red), then implement `calculateDiscount` until all pass (Green), then refactor the lookup table if needed.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Test behaviour, not implementation.** Avoid asserting on internal state or private method calls — test what the function *returns* or *does* from the caller's perspective. If you refactor internals without changing the public contract, all tests should still pass. Tests that break on every refactor are a maintenance burden, not a safety net. Also: keep each test case independent — never let one test rely on state set by a previous test.

items: The **test pyramid** prescribes many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few slow E2E tests — this maximises coverage while minimising CI time.
**TDD red-green-refactor** forces small testable units and produces a complete test suite as a development by-product, not an afterthought.
**Mocks and dependency injection** keep unit tests isolated from external services — tests run in milliseconds with no network or database required.
**CI/CD** runs lint, tests, and build on every push, blocking merges on failure and ensuring only verified code reaches production.
**Coverage thresholds** (80%+ branch coverage is a common target) enforce a minimum quality floor, but 100% coverage is not the goal — testing critical paths and edge cases is.

quiz.question: In the test pyramid, which layer should have the most tests?
options: E2E tests
Integration tests
Unit tests
Manual tests
quiz.explanation: Unit tests are the base of the pyramid — fastest, cheapest, and most numerous. They test functions in isolation in milliseconds. E2E tests are at the top: fewest, slowest, most realistic.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of the TDD cycle?
options: Write code → write test → refactor
Write test → make it pass → refactor
Refactor → write test → make it pass
Write test → refactor → make it pass
quiz.explanation: Red (write a failing test) → Green (write minimum code to pass) → Refactor (clean up without breaking tests). This is the canonical red-green-refactor cycle.

quiz.question: Why are mocks used in unit tests?
options: To make tests run in a realistic production environment.
To isolate the unit under test from external dependencies like databases and HTTP services.
To increase code coverage without writing real assertions.
To replace the function under test with a simplified version.
quiz.explanation: Mocks replace real dependencies (network, DB) with controlled fakes. This makes tests deterministic, fast, and independent of infrastructure — the hallmarks of a good unit test.

quiz.question: What does CI (Continuous Integration) primarily ensure?
options: Code is automatically deployed to production on every commit.
Every developer works on a separate long-lived branch.
Code changes are automatically built and tested on every push, catching integration issues early.
Coverage reports are sent to the team manager daily.
quiz.explanation: CI automatically runs build and tests on each push, catching broken code before it reaches the main branch. This keeps the codebase in a consistently working state.

quiz.question: Which Jest assertion is preferred for comparing floating-point results?
options: toEqual(29.997)
toBeCloseTo(29.997, 2)
toStrictEqual(29.997)
quiz.explanation: `toBeCloseTo(expected, decimalPlaces)` handles floating-point imprecision. `toBe` uses strict equality which can fail due to IEEE 754 representation errors (e.g. 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3).

quiz.question: What distinguishes an integration test from a unit test?
options: Integration tests use mocks; unit tests use real dependencies.
Integration tests are written by QA; unit tests are written by developers.
Integration tests wire together real components (e.g. service + database); unit tests test in isolation.
Integration tests only run in production environments.
quiz.explanation: Integration tests use real implementations of at least two components together — catching interface mismatches that mocks cannot reveal. Unit tests isolate the single function/class under test.

quiz.question: What is the main drawback of E2E tests compared to unit tests?
options: E2E tests cannot test authentication flows.
E2E tests only work in local environments.
E2E tests are slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain.
E2E tests do not verify real user behaviour.
quiz.explanation: E2E tests drive real browsers or HTTP clients, making them slow (minutes per run) and brittle (minor UI changes break selectors). They should be reserved for critical user paths.

quiz.question: A jest.spyOn call lets you:
options: Replace an entire module with a stub.
Observe how a real method is called (arguments, call count) without replacing its implementation.
Automatically generate test data for a function.
Skip a test case conditionally.
quiz.explanation: `jest.spyOn` wraps the original method to record calls while still running it. You can then assert `toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)` without stubbing the implementation. Use `mockImplementation` to also replace the behaviour.

quiz.question: A CI pipeline is configured to block merges when tests fail. What is the primary benefit?
options: It prevents developers from pushing code on Fridays.
It ensures broken code never reaches the main branch, keeping the codebase always deployable.
It automatically fixes failing tests.
It reduces the need to write tests because CI catches bugs.
quiz.explanation: Blocking merges on test failure enforces the invariant that the main branch is always green (passing). This is the foundation of continuous delivery — you can deploy from main at any time.

quiz.question: What does it mean to 'test behaviour, not implementation'?
options: Only test public API return values and side effects, not internal state or private methods.
Always write tests after the implementation is complete.
Mock all dependencies so tests never touch real code.
Ensure tests cover every line of code, including private methods.
quiz.explanation: Testing behaviour means asserting on what the function returns or does from the caller's perspective. If you refactor internals without changing the public contract, all tests should still pass — tests that break on every internal change are fragile.
